seed_germination.title: Seed-to-Seedling Sequence Lab
seed_germination.principle: Germination is a developmental sequence driven by hydration, metabolism, embryo growth, and emergence. Stage is more informative than elapsed time alone.

stages.label: Dry seed
stages.visible: Intact seed coat; no radicle visible.
stages.biology: The mature seed is metabolically quiet compared with active germination. Viability depends on embryo condition and storage history.
stages.observe: Seed coat integrity, storage history, obvious damage or mold.

stages.label: Imbibition
stages.visible: Seed hydrates and swells before visible emergence.
stages.biology: Water uptake rehydrates tissues and supports renewed enzyme and metabolic activity.
stages.observe: Consistent moisture without prolonged waterlogging; temperature and oxygen context.

stages.label: Seed coat split
stages.visible: The testa opens as the embryo expands.
stages.biology: Embryo growth produces enough force to separate the seed coat as germination progresses.
stages.observe: Do not confuse natural splitting with physical damage or decay.

stages.label: Radicle emergence
stages.visible: The embryonic root exits first and grows downward relative to gravity.
stages.biology: The radicle establishes the first root axis and begins anchorage and water uptake.
stages.observe: Radicle color, direction, damage, and whether surrounding media remains aerated.

stages.label: Shoot emergence
stages.visible: Hypocotyl elongation lifts the seedling toward the surface.
stages.biology: Stored seed reserves support early growth while the seedling transitions toward photosynthetic independence.
stages.observe: Stem stretch, media resistance, light availability after emergence, and damping-off symptoms.

stages.label: Cotyledons open
stages.visible: Cotyledons expand and the first true leaves begin forming.
stages.biology: Photosynthesis increases while the root system and first true leaves take over from seed reserves.
stages.observe: Cotyledon color, first true leaf shape, stem posture, root-zone moisture, and early growth rate.

nodes_branching.title: Canopy Architecture Lab
nodes_branching.principle: Branching pattern is shaped by genetics, light, resource status, hormones, node development, and training. Training changes architecture; it does not create energy by itself.

modes.label: Natural
modes.effect: The main shoot remains dominant while axillary branches develop according to genotype and environment.
modes.watch: Internode length, branch angle, light distribution, and vigor.

modes.label: Topping
modes.effect: Removing the shoot apex interrupts apical dominance and allows nearby axillary branches to compete more strongly for growth.
modes.watch: Recovery at the cut, symmetry of responding branches, and plant vigor before further training.

modes.label: LST
modes.effect: Bending and positioning shoots changes orientation and light exposure without removing the main apex.
modes.watch: Stem stress, tie pressure, branch spacing, and whether the canopy actually receives more even light.

modes.label: SCROG
modes.effect: A screen is used to distribute many shoots across a wider horizontal canopy so growing points occupy separate light zones.
modes.watch: Crowding below the screen, airflow, access, branch support, and continued stretch.

leaves.title: Leaf Pattern Interpretation Lab
leaves.principle: A leaf symptom is a pattern to describe before it is a cause to name. Location, distribution, progression, root-zone context, pests, and environment determine what the pattern means.

patterns.label: Healthy baseline
patterns.description: Uniform green appropriate to the cultivar, intact margins, normal posture, and no expanding lesions.
firstChecks: Use this as the visual baseline

patterns.label: Interveinal chlorosis
patterns.description: Leaf tissue between veins becomes lighter while veins remain comparatively greener.
firstChecks: Check pH, EC, roots, and recent feed history

patterns.label: Marginal necrosis
patterns.description: Dead or browning tissue develops along leaf edges or serrations.
firstChecks: Heat, airflow, disease, and root-zone context

patterns.label: Tip burn
patterns.description: Damage begins at leaflet tips and may progress inward if the underlying stress continues.
firstChecks: Is the damage uniform across the canopy?
Look for simultaneous margin or root symptoms

patterns.label: Curl / posture change
patterns.description: Tacoing, canoeing, clawing, drooping, twisting, or cupping changes leaf orientation without being a diagnosis by itself.
firstChecks: Light cycle timing, moisture status, temperature, RH, and airflow

patterns.label: Stippling / feeding marks
patterns.description: Many small pale points or silvered areas can indicate surface or cell-feeding damage, but magnified inspection is needed.
firstChecks: Look for webbing, insects, eggs, frass, or silvering

environment_overlay.title: Environment Relationship Lab
environment_overlay.principle: The plant experiences a coupled environment. Light changes leaf energy load; temperature and humidity shape evaporative demand; airflow alters boundary layers; root water supply must support the canopy response.

factors.label: Light / PPFD
factors.summary: More incident light can increase photosynthetic opportunity and leaf energy load. Response depends on CO₂, temperature, water supply, nutrition, acclimation, and genetics.

factors.label: Leaf temperature
factors.summary: Leaf temperature can differ from air temperature and directly affects saturation vapor pressure at the leaf surface and therefore plant evaporative demand.

factors.label: Relative humidity
factors.summary: RH describes air moisture relative to temperature. Its biological effect must be interpreted with leaf temperature and air temperature rather than in isolation.

factors.label: VPD
factors.summary: VPD represents the vapor-pressure difference driving transpiration. It is a derived relationship, not a standalone environmental knob.

factors.label: Airflow
factors.summary: Air movement influences leaf boundary layers, heat exchange, gas exchange, and local humidity. Excessive or poorly distributed airflow can also stress tissue.

factors.label: Root water supply
factors.summary: Canopy demand must be matched by root water uptake. Media moisture, oxygen, EC, roots, and irrigation timing all affect the supply side.

factors.label: CO₂
factors.summary: CO₂ availability interacts with light and temperature in photosynthesis. Added CO₂ does not compensate for poor water, light, temperature, or root-zone management.

factors.label: Root-zone EC
factors.summary: Ionic concentration affects osmotic conditions around roots and must be interpreted with irrigation, dryback, media, crop stage, and measurement method.

diagnostic_overlay.title: Observation-First Diagnostic Lab
diagnostic_overlay.principle: The goal is not to guess a deficiency from a picture. Build an evidence profile first, then rank plausible causes and decide what measurement or inspection would discriminate between them.
speeds: rapid within a day or two
